title: Freedom House and the R.T. Weatherman Foundation Announce Partnership to Advocate for the Release of Hong Kong Political Prisoner Joshua Wong
content:
Washington, DC, and London, UK—Freedom House and the R.T. Weatherman Foundation are pleased to announce a partnership to advocate for the release of Hong Kong prodemocracy advocate and political prisoner Joshua Wong. As part of this work, Freedom House’s Fred Hiatt Program to Free Political Prisoners is formally adopting Wong’s case.

Joshua Wong is a prominent leader in Hong Kong’s prodemocracy movement whose activism has received international attention and acclaim. He co-founded the student group Scholarism, was a key leader in the 2014 Umbrella Movement protests in which Hong Kongers demanded free and fair elections, and co-founded the prodemocracy political party Demosistō. As a result of his activism, he has been imprisoned several times, including continuously since November 2020. On September 2, he is expected to plead guilty to charges under Hong Kong’s notorious National Security Law, which has contributed to the rapid deterioration of basic freedoms in the territory.

title: Political Prisoners Watch: Why Human Rights and Democracy Are the Only Way Forward for Cameroon
content:
Tsi Conrad is a journalist in Cameroon who has been imprisoned for over 9.5 years. In this piece written from prison, Tsi shares his thoughts on Cameroon’s now decade-long Anglophone crisis: the violent conflict between the Francophone-dominated government and the English-speaking regions that has left thousands dead and millions displaced. Cameroon’s president Paul Biya—who has been in power since 1982, enabled by the elimination of constitutional term limits in 2011—has been unwilling or unable to secure a cease-fire. Freedom House’s Fred Hiatt Program to Free Political Prisoners has adopted Tsi’s case and has been advocating for his release.


By Tsi Conrad, Cameroonian journalist, political prisoner

title: Statement on the Announcement of Reform and Renewal of the Supreme Court of Justice within the Framework of the Dialogue Table
content:
The undersigned civil society organizations take note of the joint statement issued on August 12 by representatives of the government and the National Assembly elected in 2015, announcing the launch of a process to reform the Organic Law of the Supreme Court of Justice (LOTSJ) and to renew all of its justices.

We take note of this announcement with particular attention, as it places at the center of the institutional re-establishment agenda precisely the structural issue that we have identified for years as an unavoidable condition for any meaningful change in Venezuela: the role played by the Judiciary, and particularly the Supreme Court of Justice (TSJ), as an instrument of repression, political persecution, and the progressive dismantling of the rule of law. The fact that judicial reform is explicitly included in the agenda of this dialogue table is, in itself, an acknowledgment of a reality that civil society has consistently documented. The announcement made by the dialogue table confirms the continued relevance and urgency of our longstanding warnings.

title: Values & Interests: Democracy as a Moral Principle
content:
The Carnegie Council for Ethics in International Affairs will host a discussion, the latest in their Values & Interests series, featuring a fireside chat and Q&A between Freedom House CEO Jamie Fly and Carnegie Council President Joel Rosenthal.

Together, Rosenthal and Fly will interrogate why democracy is both a moral and a political principle, the regression of freedom globally, and what can be done to counter the new wave of autocrats and illiberal actors.

The event will feature a 60-minute panel discussion and audience Q&A.

Register to attend virtually on the Carnegie Council website.

title: The Political Prisoners Xi Jinping Doesn't Want the World to See
content:
Register
 

As Chinese leader Xi Jinping prepares to visit Washington in September, much of the public conversation will focus on trade, security, technology, and strategic competition. Yet no discussion of the U.S.-China relationship is complete without acknowledging the Chinese Communist Party's systematic assault on fundamental freedoms. Behind every statistic is a person: a journalist imprisoned for telling the truth, a pastor jailed for practicing his faith, a democracy advocate sentenced for demanding free elections, a Uyghur or Tibetan detained for their identity, or a family separated for exercising basic human rights.

title: Update from Freedom House CEO Jamie Fly: Two Political Prisoners Released, More Successes in the Fight for Global Freedom
content:
July 2026 brought real, tangible wins for those on the frontlines of freedom.

Pastor Jin is Free
On July 4, Pastor Ezra Jin—who founded and led Zion Church, one of China’s largest underground house churches—arrived in the United States and was reunited with his family after spending nine months in a Chinese prison for practicing and sharing his Christian faith. Freedom House was deeply involved in the advocacy effort to free him. President Trump raised the case directly with Xi Jinping at the May summit in Beijing. Weeks later, Pastor Jin was released and flown to Los Angeles where he was greeted by his family, including his one-month-old grandson Ezra, named after him. We continue to press for the release of fellow Zion Church members and others still detained by the Chinese Communist Party, including media publisher and prodemocracy advocate Jimmy Lai, scholar and US citizen U Min Zin, and prodemocracy activist and politician Joshua Wong.

title: TNR Watch: Cyberattacks as a Tactic of Digital Transnational Repression
content: Cat-and-mouse game: Exiled journalists and media outlets are exposed to malicious web activity at a rate four times higher than media organizations overall. This is one of the findings of a report recently released by Cloudflare based on data collected as part of the company’s Project Galileo, which offers free services to at-risk public interest groups. The report finds that around 5 percent of the 41 billion requests directed to exile journalism websites between February 2025 and January 2026 were harmful and sought to disrupt the outlets’ connections to their readers. Tactics employed to paralyze these platforms included distributed-denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, website-vulnerability attacks, and phishing attempts; the sites were also made inaccessible via internet shutdowns.

title: Freedom In Focus: Elections Abolished in Nicaragua
content:
Nicaraguans living in Costa Rica protest against the government of Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega in 2021. (Photo: Ezequiel Becerra/AFP via Getty Images)

On July 19, during a ceremony commemorating the 47th anniversary of the Sandinista Revolution, Daniel Ortega boldly declared the elimination of elections in Nicaragua, saying, “Forget it; there won't be elections here again.” Referring to the opposition and other regime critics, the 80-year-old dictator asserted that they would never again have the opportunity to take control of the government and “seize power.” 

Freedom House has closely tracked Nicaragua’s transition from a fragile democracy to an outright autocracy under Ortega’s authoritarian rule. Freedom in the World data shows that the country had the second-largest deterioration in political rights and civil liberties since 2005, declining by a staggering 49 points on the survey’s 100-point scale. In light of Ortega’s announcement, Freedom House’s experts and analysis were called on to help explain what’s at stake.
